summary: This BusinessWorld article, the second in a series following the 2nd SGV Tax Symposium, outlines the Philippine strategy for sustainable development under the Philippine Development Plan (PDP) 2023-2028. It covers investment-led growth, human capital and infrastructure, fiscal consolidation and debt, inflation control, and climate resilience. The author argues the private sector will be an important catalyst in achieving the goals.
one_line: An SGV article reviewing the Philippine Development Plan 2023-2028 strategy on growth, infrastructure, debt, inflation and climate resilience for sustainable development.
key_facts: The Philippine Development Plan (PDP) 2023-2028 aims to reinvigorate job creation and accelerate poverty reduction by steering the economy back to a high-growth path.
To reach upper middle-income status the Philippines needs a GNI per capita of at least $4,466; in 2022 it achieved $3,950.
The government aims to cut poverty from 18.1% in 2021 to single digits by 2028, with growth pencilled between 6.5% and 8%.
Growth is expected to be investment-led through the CREATE law and amendments to the Public Service Act, Foreign Investment Act and Retail Trade Liberalization Act.
The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) is already in force for the Philippines and could help it become a regional manufacturing hub.
The government aims to sustain infrastructure spending at 5-6% of GDP through 2028 while narrowing the deficit to 3% of GDP from 7.3% in 2022.
Debt-to-GDP was nearly 61% in 2022 and is targeted at no more than 53% by 2028; it was below 40% before the pandemic.
Planned revenue measures include digitalization of tax collection, VAT on digital service providers and excise tax on sweetened beverages and junk food.
Inflation averaged 6.6% in the first nine months of 2023, above the BSP target range of 2-4%.
Marcos signed Executive Order No. 28 in May, forming the Inter-Agency Committee on Inflation and Market Outlook.
The government distributed 28,000 new tools and machinery to farmers and laid an additional 600 km of farm-to-market roads supporting 14 million hectares of farmland.
The World Risk Index 2022 identifies the Philippines as the most disaster-prone country in the world.
The government envisions by 2028 greater climate and disaster resilience, enhanced ecosystem resilience and a low-carbon economy transition.
The Public-Private Partnership (PPP) Act awaited President Marcos' signature and is expected to mobilize private resources for infrastructure.
